It's 24 December 2032, 2 p.m. Tonight the whole family is coming to Ludwig's: Thomas with his wife and children from Munich, and Sabine, Lena's mother, from Potsdam. Lena is checking the list.
The tree is decorated. Since this morning. Ludwig moved every bauble three times.
Because they were hung wrong. Ingrid always put the red baubles at the bottom and the gold ones at the top.

The red cabbage and the dumplings?

German clearly distinguishes the action in progress (werden + participle) from the resulting state (sein + participle):
Der Tisch wird gedeckt. (the table is being laid)
Der Tisch ist gedeckt. (the table is laid)
Die Gans wird gebraten. (the goose is being roasted)
Die Gans ist gebraten. (the goose is roasted)
Das Café wird geschlossen. (is being closed)
Test question: is something happening NOW (process), or am I describing how things LOOK (state)? “Wird” = a film, “ist” = a photo.
2. The forms of the state passive
Bis sechs muss alles fertig gekocht sein.

Don't confuse the state passive with the Perfekt of verbs of motion: “Er ist gegangen” (he has left — active Perfekt) versus “Die Tür ist geöffnet” (the door is open — state). The first one has a subject that does the action.
Many participles are used almost like ordinary adjectives after “sein”:
And as an adjective in front of the noun, with an ending: der geschmückte Baum, die gebratene Gans, ein reservierter Tisch.
With the state passive you usually don't say who did the action — only the result matters. If you want to say it, switch to the process passive or to the active:
The tree is decorated. (it doesn't matter by whom)
The tree was decorated by Ludwig.
The table is being laid now.
Unfortunately the hotel is fully booked.

At six everything was ready. The table was laid, with Ingrid's white tablecloth and the good china with the blue rim, which was only taken out of the cupboard at Christmas. The candles were lit. The tree was decorated, the red baubles at the bottom, the gold ones at the top, as was proper. The goose was roasted and smelt wonderful throughout the ground-floor flat, all the way to the stairwell, all the way to the courtyard. Fritz lay in front of the stove pretending to sleep, but his nose twitched every time someone opened the kitchen door.

All afternoon there had been work going on in the house. Andrei had stuffed the goose, with apples, onions and marjoram, following the recipe in Ingrid's old cookbook, whose pages were full of grease stains and pencil notes. Lena had cleaned the flat, twice, because after the first time Ludwig had run his finger over the tiled stove and found dust. Mara and Jakob had carried the chairs down from their flat, because twelve people wouldn't fit at Ludwig's table, and Kuba and Ola had folded the napkins into little stars, following an online tutorial that they had misunderstood three times.

Sabine arrived first, from Potsdam, on the regional train with a basket full of home-made biscuits. She was Ludwig's daughter, Lena's mother, a quiet woman of fifty-two, a librarian, who talked like Ingrid and laughed like Ludwig. She hugged her father for a long time, then her daughter, then Andrei, whom she now called “my son-in-law”, even though officially he wasn't yet. Andrei blushed every time. Lena pretended not to have heard.

Thomas arrived at half past six, with his wife, Anja, and their three children, who were no longer children: Paul, twenty-three, a student in Vienna, Marie, twenty, at nursing school in Munich, and Leo, seventeen, who was taller than everyone else in the room and so shy that he barely said hello. They had driven from Munich, seven hours, with two traffic jams and a break at a motorway service area, where Leo had eaten a sausage he now regretted, because he could smell the goose.

Thomas was fifty-seven, an engineer at a big company, grey-haired, with Ludwig's hands and Ingrid's eyes. Four years ago, on Ludwig's eightieth birthday, father and son had made up after a long quarrel, at the little kitchen table, over coffee from the cups with the blue flowers. Since then they had talked on the phone every Sunday. But Thomas rarely came to Berlin, two or three times a year, and every time he left, Ludwig was quiet for two days.

Thomas looked around the new flat. He had never been here, on the ground floor. He only knew the old flat on the first floor, where he had lived for another two years after the move in 1995, before he went off to study in Munich. He saw Ingrid's armchair by the window, the tiled stove, the slice of wood with the eighty rings above it, and then the little tin box on the shelf that Ludwig had told him about on the phone. “It's lovely here, Dad,” he said quietly. “Lovelier than upstairs.” Ludwig nodded. “Downstairs you're closer to the ground,” he said. “At my age that's not a bad thought.”

The meal lasted three hours. There was a lot of laughing and even more eating. Marie and Lena, who for years had only seen each other in photos, sat next to each other and talked as if they were sisters. Paul was discussing artificial intelligence with Andrei. Anja was listening to Sabine explain the biscuit recipe. And Leo, shy Leo, sat next to Ludwig and listened to his grandfather telling stories about line 46, open-mouthed, as if he were hearing the story for the first time. Which was true. Nobody had ever told it to him.
Outside the rain had stopped, and through the window you could see the lights in the courtyard, where someone had hung a string of fairy lights in the old chestnut tree.

Anja, who was from Bavaria, was surprised that there was goose already on Christmas Eve. “At home we have frankfurters with potato salad today,” she said. “The goose only comes tomorrow.” Ludwig laughed. “With us it was always like this. Ingrid didn't want to cook on Christmas Day. She wanted to sit in her armchair and read the books she'd been given. All day. And woe betide anyone who disturbed her.” Sabine nodded. “That's right. On the twenty-fifth we children were only allowed to whisper. It was the quietest day of the year.”

At one point Ludwig put down his fork and looked at his youngest grandson. “Leo,” he said, “what do you actually want to be?” Leo blushed and looked at his plate. “I don't know,” he mumbled. “Everyone says I should become an engineer, like Dad. But I…” He stopped. “But?” asked Ludwig. Leo glanced briefly at his father, then back at his plate. “I like riding the tram,” he said, so quietly that you could barely hear him. “In Munich. I always sit right at the front, behind the driver.” Ludwig smiled, and Thomas, at the other end of the table, had heard and said nothing, but he smiled too.

Then came the presents. The presents were piled up under the tree, in coloured paper, with names on little cards. There were books and scarves and a bottle of Romanian țuică, sent by Dan, Andrei's father, from Sibiu, with a note in very bad German, which everyone read out loud. And right at the end, when all the presents had been unwrapped, Ludwig got up, went into the bedroom and came back with a small parcel. It was wrapped very clumsily, in newspaper, with too much sticky tape. You could see straight away that it had been wrapped by someone who hadn't done this for decades.
Thomas. This is for you. You got it once before, at Christmas in 1980. You were five. Then it got lost, in the move in 1995. I found it again last month. In a crate I never unpacked.

Thomas opened the parcel slowly. Inside was a small wooden tram, red and beige, with four wheels that still turned and a tiny bell on the roof. On one side, painted with a fine brush, it said: “46”. Ludwig had built it himself, in the autumn of 1980, at night, in the workshop at the depot, out of scraps of wood. A quarter of a century earlier, his own father had built him a similar one.

“I remember,” said Thomas quietly, and his voice suddenly sounded young. “I took it everywhere with me. To nursery, to bed, into the bath. Mum used to tell me off, because the paint was coming off. And then, at some point, I stopped playing with it, because I was too big. And then it disappeared and I never thought about it again. Until now.” He pressed the little bell. “It sounds exactly the same.”

Thomas said nothing for a long time. He turned the little tram in his hands, let the wheels run, carefully pressed the tiny bell, which gave a thin, clear sound. Then he looked at his father, with wet eyes, and said something nobody expected, not even Anja, who knew, but hadn't thought he would say it tonight.

Dad, I have some news too. My company is opening a new factory in Berlin in the spring, in Adlershof. They're looking for a director. I applied without telling you. Last week the answer came: yes. The contract is already signed. From April we'll be living in Berlin again. I'm coming home.

It was very quiet in the room. All you could hear was the candles crackling and Fritz sighing under the table. Then Ludwig stood up, slowly, leaning on his stick, walked round the table and hugged his son, the way he had last hugged him when Thomas was five and had found a wooden tram under the tree. Sabine was crying. Lena was crying. Anja was crying. And Leo, shy Leo, picked up the little tram, which had been left on the table, and very gently pressed the bell. Once. For everyone.

Late at night, when everyone had gone or was asleep, Ludwig sat alone at the table for a while, among the empty glasses and the crumpled wrapping paper. Thomas had taken the little wooden tram. He'd said he wanted to put it in his new office in Adlershof, on his desk, so that everyone could see where he came from. Ludwig blew out the last candle and looked towards the window, behind which, in the courtyard, it was starting to snow. “You see, Ingrid,” he said quietly. “He's coming home.”
